Crime recording and monitoring is essential in ensuring peace and security within a community. As such, police departments are reliant on accurate data and well-maintained records of crimes committed to track down and prosecute offenders. It is therefore important that police departments have proper and updated records of all crimes. With the rise of modern technology, most organizations and government agencies are embracing technology to manage and store data digitally and make it easily accessible. Some organizations are using crime mapping technology also known as GIS to record and monitor crime patterns and locations on maps.

The Philippine National Police in the Koronadal is a government agency tasked with providing security to the people of Koronadal City in South Cotabato. Their duty includes regulating and enforcing laws in the city and taking action after a crime or a report of a crime has been confirmed. The police station is answerable to the Local Government Unit of the city and provides services such as recording, documenting and investigating criminal activity and cases and providing assistance
to crime prevention and response within the region.

At present, PNP Koronadal Station utilizes a computerized but manual method in recording and monitoring of crime incident. Encoding of data in computer database is done manually while some data are retrieved from written or manual reports. Information such as type of offense committed, date and time of incident, and location of incident among others are being recorded and stored for monitoring, reference and report generation purposes. In addition, the location of the incident is manually recorded or provided in written or narrative form.

However, the current process has a lot of drawbacks in terms of recording and monitoring of crime. The process of encoding crime incident details is tedious and can cause missing information, incorrect recording, and errors. The retrieval of past crime incident records might be difficult when the file is not properly indexed. Determining the hotspots is difficult due to the absence of a map feature where the investigator is able to indicate the approximate location or exact spot of the crime occurrence. A report generation based on type of crime, barangay, status, and period of occurrence requires additional time and effort.

These problems negatively affect the efficiency of the PNP Koronadal Station in addressing crime-related issues. Police personnel waste a lot of their time by organizing and preparing reports instead of doing actual supervisory duties. Moreover, the process of accessing information is too slow, making it difficult for the officers to make decisions regarding crime patterns. In addition, for the managing body and external agencies, the lack of proper reporting delays the process of planning and decision-making related to achieving public safety.

he researchers suggest developing a Web-Based Crime Mapping System with GIS Integration for the Philippine National Police Koronadal Station to address the identified issues. The system will provide features that will allow them to properly store, manage, and monitor the collected data. It will enable the officers to enter information about crime incidents, visualize the recorded incidents on a map, and generate reports in terms of barangay and hotspots. Ultimately, this proposed information system will support the station in improving its current status and helping it perform its duties more efficiently in order to achieve peace and order in the city.

The aim of the proposed Web-Based Crime Mapping System with GIS Integration is to enhance the recording, monitoring, and reporting of crimes in Philippine National Police Koronadal Station. This project is proposed to solve the problems in the current system, which are: time-consuming encoding process, disorganized, and non-systematized records and files, inability to easily retrieve information about incidents, lack of mapping tools, delay in report generation, and no system to monitor crime records. It is also expected that this project will assist PNP Koronadal Station in organizing and maintaining accurate data, minimizing manual work, and providing timely information that will aid the city in attaining peace and order.

The proposed project is a web-based crime mapping system that will enable authorized users of the Philippine National Police Koronadal Station, including the administrator, police officers, investigators, and LGU viewers, to record and manage crime incident data, track blotter workflow status, store records in a database, display incidents on the map, view records according to barangay, identify high-crime areas, upload relevant evidence, monitor audit logs, and generate reports.

The Web-Based Crime Mapping System with GIS Integration can help the Philippine National Police Koronadal Station achieve better organization of crime records, monitoring, and reporting through the system’s features. The PNP Koronadal can retrieve and analyze the data faster and more efficient than before, making the processing of related reports easier. The system can also make it more convenient for authorized users to document and report cases using the system. The Web-Based Crime Mapping System with GIS Integration can aid the PNP Koronadal in providing reliable data for planning, monitoring, and decision-making purposes for the safety of the city.

The proposed system is subject to the following limitations:
Limited for PNP Koronadal Station Only -
The system is designed specifically for the Philippine National Police Koronadal Station and may require modification before it can be used by other police stations or agencies.
The system covers crime incidents recorded within Koronadal City only.
The system can only be accessed by registered users such as administrators, police officers, investigators, and LGU viewers.
The system does not allow citizens or anonymous users to directly submit crime reports.
The web-based system requires a working server and stable internet or local network connection to access records and map-related features.
The system is available as a web-based application only and does not include a dedicated Android or iOS mobile application.
No SMS or Incident Email Notification -
The system does not support SMS or email notifications for incident updates. However, email is used only for account recovery through password reset OTP verification.

The system does not connect with external government systems, national police databases, LGU systems, or other third-party data platforms. Mapping services may be used only for map visualization and location display.
The system supports crime recording, mapping, hotspot viewing, and analytics, but it does not include artificial intelligence, machine learning, or automated crime prediction.
The system is intended only to support crime recording, monitoring, mapping, and reporting, and should not replace official police investigation procedures or legal documentation processes.

GIS&T in Criminal Justice and Law Enforcement

Morgan et al. (2022) stated that Geographic information science and technology (GIS&T) have become increasingly essential in contemporary criminal justice and law enforcement because of its innovative applications in acquiring, storing, analyzing, and displaying geographical information related to criminal cases. Morgan et al. (2022) explicated that crimes are committed at particular places and under specific conditions. Therefore, it is fundamental to understand the locations and circumstances of criminal incidents to effectively respond to crime problems using available resources. The chapter by Morgan et al. (2022) articulated that GIS&T is critical in analyzing and visualizing geographical information related to
criminal cases for efficient decision-making and implementation of effective strategies at different levels.

Morgan et al. (2022) elaborated on the history of the application of GIS&T in criminal justice and explained how far it has evolved and its significance in the modern processing of crime. According to Morgan et al. (2022), the initial application of GIS&T in criminal justice was in manually marking crime location spots on a map for better representation and visualization. Morgan et al. (2022) asserted that with the evolution of geographic technology, GIS has become instrumental in analyzing statistical data, processing crime maps, identifying hotspots, and addressing crime-related issues such as patterns of offenders, and examining the relationship between environmental attributes and criminal activity. Morgan et al. (2022) explicated that modern technologies have made it possible to utilize mapping technology, digital data, spatial databases, web-enabled geographic information systems, imaging systems, and satellite systems in analyzing and responding to criminal incidents. This is fundamental in helping law enforcers monitor and respond to emerging criminal activities promptly, and the overall effect is enhanced public safety. Morgan et al. (2022) concluded that GIS has become an integral part of modern law enforcement and criminal intelligence analysis because of its ability to offer analytical and decision-making capabilities when addressing crime control and security issues.

In his discussion, Morgan et al. (2022) identified several theories that provide a theoretical basis for applying GIS&T in criminal justice, namely, Environmental Criminology, Crime Pattern Theory, Routine Activity Theory, and Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design. Morgan et al. (2022) explained that these theories highlight the significance of locations and the environment in which crimes occur. They also help in explaining how the physical and social environments influence criminal activity, with little

emphasis on the role of offenders. According to Morgan et al. (2022), the theories have helped crime analysts understand the role of land use, roads, buildings, shops, homes, access to and from crime scenes, and other elements that contribute to criminal activities. Morgan et al. (2022) asserted that by combining geographical analysis with criminological theories, law enforcers and policymakers can gain profound insights into the causes and correlates of criminal activity. Therefore, the application of these theories plays a significant role in helping agencies and policymakers make informed evidence-based policies and operational decisions related to crime prevention and control.

Morgan et al. (2022) explained that there has been an exponential rise in the use of web-based GIS in supporting criminal intelligence analysis and responding to public safety issues in the modern era. According to Morgan et al. (2022), web-based GIS enables authorized users, partners, and the public to collaborate in addressing crime problems by accessing the required information using user-friendly interfaces and tools available online. This is critical in enhancing transparency by making the information accessible and available whenever it is needed while facilitating effective coordination of criminal intelligence analysis activities among law enforcers, authorities, academics, and the public. Morgan et al. (2022) asserted that web-based GIS is increasingly being used to disseminate crime-related information and support decision-making at various levels of implementation while offering an opportunity to share location-based information and respond promptly to emerging issues. The overall effect of adopting web-based GIS technologies is that they facilitate seamless coordination in supporting public safety operations through enhanced exchange and visualization of geographical information related to criminal activity.

In their final discussion, Morgan et al. (2022) emphasized that GIS&T has revolutionized the criminal justice system by introducing state-of-the-art technology in acquiring, analyzing and visualizing geographical data related to crime. Morgan et al. (2022) argued that modern GIS&T has evolved from mapping and presenting data to offering analytical capabilities that support predicting, responding, and preventing crime. According to Morgan et al. (2022), GIS is now integral to criminal intelligence analysis in supporting hotspot analysis, patrol operations, emergency response, and implementing effective strategies and policies to enhance public safety. The authors concluded that with new innovations in GIS technology, web-enabled GIS technologies will be instrumental in the future of crime mapping and analysis as they enhance decision-making and support efficient strategies to increase public safety while promoting coexistence and sustainable development.

The authors stressed the significance of crime as a social problem that substantially impacts the lives of people and communities. and Colak (2023), in particular, examined the interrelations between burglaries and the urban environment in the city of Trabzon, Turkey. Using the tools of GIS and machine learning, the authors predicted possible crimes and investigated how burglaries are affected by different environmental variables. It was identified that the Random Forest Regression (RFR) model demonstrated better results than the Support Vector Regression (SVR) algorithm. Indeed, RFR yielded an R2 value of 78%, while the R2 value of SVR was 71%. In addition, the analysis revealed that building height, floor area ratio, building density, and street intersection density have the most profound impact on burglaries, whereas the percentage of park area in comparison to residential area has a negligible effect on the incidents. The authors concluded that using the principles of GIS and regression models helps appropriately predict burglaries while providing insight into the influence of the urban environment on criminal activity.

and Colak (2023) noted that researchers could also utilize Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) to analyze the influence of the built environment on the patterns of criminal activity. They mentioned that CPTED is a theoretical basis that assists in developing and implementing policies that improve the impact of the built environment on citizen safety and decrease threats and risks of incidents. In other words, CPTED principles help design specific areas considering the entry and exit of people, visibility within the site, surveillance rates, control of natural and artificial landscapes, and other elements that could limit the possibility of crimes. Moreover, the authors identified Crime Pattern Theory, Routine Activity Theory, Defensible Space Theory, and

Space Syntax as additional concepts that highlight the necessity to consider the urban environment for better protection of the public and safer communities. The integration of GIS and CPTED allows researchers to address the role of spatial analysis and better understand the impact of different built-environment features, such as streets, roads, buildings, land use, density, lighting, and spaces, on the patterns and incidents of crime.

and Colak (2023) described their own methodology that was used to predict burglaries and identify the influence of the urban environment on them. The authors used burglary-related data collected by the Trabzon Police Department for the past five years and integrated it with physical evidence obtained from cadastral, municipal departments, and GIS laboratories. In particular, the data concerning crime incidents was geocoded and stored in a GIS database. Then, the authors divided the study area into 200 x 200 m grids to improve results and utilized the collected geographical data about the urban environment. It was subjected to spatial analysis with the help of GIS software. Finally, the acquired findings were examined using machine learning in Python Scikit-learn. The authors concluded that the combination of GIS and machine learning could be used as a reliable method to predict burglary crimes and examine the impact of different built-environment factors. In addition, the article stressed the necessity of further development of innovative, interactive, web-based crime analysis tools based on GIS, machine learning algorithms, and crime prevention theories to ensure safe and sustainable communities and better address the patterns of criminal activity.
Mapping Study Using the Unsupervised Learning Clustering Approach

Azis et al. (2021) assert that crime is a serious social issue that affects public safety and the country’s development. They point out that the number of criminal cases is growing rapidly and significantly in Indonesia, which requires the use of innovative analytical approaches to identify patterns and better understand crime trends. The researchers argue that traditional statistical analysis tools are not always effective in providing critical insights into crime-related data, especially when dealing with complex sets. Therefore, they suggest using data mining techniques to extract valuable information from gigantic data sets. In particular, Azis et al. (2021) propose to apply clustering algorithms to group similar types of crime and help the government and police visualize patterns associated with specific locations. Such an approach would facilitate creating appropriate policies and strategies to prevent and control further criminal activity on national levels.

In the given research, the authors used an unsupervised learning method called K-Medoids clustering analysis to examine the crime data collected from the Operations Control Bureau of the National Police Headquarters of the Republic of Indonesia and the Central Statistics Agency (BPS). Azis et al. (2021) retrieved the crime data from all provincial police regional headquarters (34 total) for the years 2017 – 2019 and used RapidMiner software to perform the clustering analysis. They determined that the Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI) was appropriate to evaluate the results of the clustering by dividing the provinces into two clusters, high-crime regions, and low-crime regions. The authors’ results indicated that six provinces fell into the category of high-crime regions while twenty-eight provinces fell into the category of low-crime regions, which demonstrated
that data mining could be used to group the relevant information together in order to visualize patterns within the data set.

The researchers also discuss the relevance of data mining and clustering to crime mapping and public safety planning. Azis et al. (2021) argue that clustering helps address crimes in provinces with comparable patterns, thus saving time and effort in determining the best crime control strategies. They provide their findings on the application of clustering in scatter plots and mapping to improve the understanding of the distribution of crimes by the authorities. The researchers conclude that the combination of crime data and spatial clustering can benefit the government in monitoring and controlling criminal activities.

Azis et al. (2021) found that using K-Medoids clustering to classify crime data resulted in successfully dividing it into high- and low-crime categories with a Davies-Bouldin Index of 0.876 (a satisfactory level of clustering). The authors noted that the discovered clusters could help the government focus on high-crime areas and emphasized the importance of using data mining and machine learning methods for analyzing crime to facilitate decision-making, strengthen crime prevention, and create intelligent crime mapping systems that would assist the authorities in planning and policing activities.

Du and Ding (2023) explained the nature and characteristics of crime by postulating that crime presents as a complex, ongoing, and dynamic social event that cannot be understood independently of time-space and environmental factors. As such, criminal acts usually demonstrate identifiable spatial and temporal patterns and emerge mainly from particular places referred to as hotspots (Du & Ding, 2023). Notably, contemporary

crime analysis practices take cognizance of this understanding of crime to ensure effective crime prevention, police resource management, and community safety. These researchers argue that the task of predicting crime entails examining historical crime data alongside environmental, socioeconomic, and social network characteristics in order to ascertain patterns likely to emerge in particular places and times.

The researchers undertook this study with the intent to engage and review published literature on the prediction of crime over a specified period of time. Hence, Du and Ding (2023) conducted a PRISMA-based systematic review of 79 articles published between 2013 and 2022, which met the inclusion criteria for this review (Du & Ding, 2023). Following peer-review and inclusion in databases of the top journals, each of the papers that were included in this review presented different aspects of crime prediction based on content, crime type, prediction approaches, and evaluation criteria. For instance, the review grouped crime prediction models and methods as short/medium/long temporal prediction, micro/

-temporal prediction, thus covering the general theory of crime prediction. The researchers also provided an overview of the most common assessment criteria used in this field, namely; Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Predictive Accuracy Index (PAI), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Accuracy, and Area Under the Curve (AUC)).

Du and Ding (2023) also identified machine learning and crime mapping as the mainstay theoretical frameworks used in contemporary crime prediction practices. According to Du and Ding (2023), researchers usually apply a range of supervised, unsupervised, and semi-supervised machine learning techniques to predict crime patterns. These machine learning algorithms include but are not limited to Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Ensemble, neural networks, and deep learning (Du & Ding, 2023). On the crime mapping front, Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and

Risk Terrain Modeling (RTM) are the most common methods used in hotspot identification, assessment of potential environmental risk factors, and representation of this information in graphical form. These researchers argue that the application of Geographic Information Systems –based data mining approaches in tandem with machine learning algorithms can help improve the identification of hotspots, which in turn enhances policing efficacy.

The researchers made several recommendations for improving crime prediction practices based on current gaps in the literature. First, Du and Ding (2023) noted the challenges associated with the current application of

-temporal data science in policing, including sparse data, limited interpretability, and the use of different evaluation criteria. As such, this reviewer recommends adopting cutting-edge deep artificial intelligence to address the sparse data challenges, including transformers. Additionally, this researcher recommends adopting XAI (Explainable Artificial Intelligence) approaches like SHAP (

) to improve model interpretability (Du & Ding, 2023). Lastly, the adoption of standardized evaluation frameworks and Reinforcement Learning to achieve policing efficacy and decision-support during the implementation phase would also help improve the effectiveness of crime prediction practices. Ultimately, Du and Ding (2023) conclude that using Geographic Information Systems and artificial intelligence –based crime prediction practices is the way forward in future criminal justice practice and research.

The Accuracy of Crime Statistics: Assessing the Impact of Police Data Bias on Geographic Crime Analysis

Buil-Gil et al. (2022) explained that police-recorded crime information is the primary source used by law enforcement agencies, governments, and researchers to understand, represent, and respond to the patterns and trends of crime. The authors emphasized that official statistics are critical in geographical crime analysis to ensure the most effective police resource allocation to hotspots. However, police-reported crime data is subject to
selection bias that decreases the accuracy of police records, especially at smaller levels of geographical aggregation.

Buil-Gil et al. (2022) highlighted the importance of micro-level analysis based on very local scales like street segments, addresses, and places in crime research. Authors explained that the distribution of crime is not random since criminal activity tends to concentrate in particular places. It was explained that a large percentage of crimes occur in only a fraction of space, and police forces acknowledge this fact and are starting to shift towards place-based policing. The authors added that crime analysis using geographical information systems (GIS) and mapping is considered an excellent approach to identifying hotspots and better allocating police resources.

Buil-Gil et al. (2022) argued that although micro-local levels of geographical analysis offer greater resolution and granularity, such information can be associated with significant measurement issues like varying levels of police-recorded crime. Authors explained that victim characteristics like age, gender, education, ethnicity, employment status, and others affect people’s willingness to report criminal activity to the authorities. Similarly, the level of police presence, surveillance, and monitoring activities, as well as general attitudes towards police and feelings of safety, are crucial determinants of reported crime in a given area. Therefore, a combination of differing police forces’ strategies, surveillance, recording practices, and residents’ perceptions of safety creates significant variations in police-reported crime statistics and an altered understanding of the crime reality in a given location.
Buil-Gil et al. (2022) conducted a simulation study to demonstrate how police data can skewer the analysis of geographical variation and distribution of crime. Authors used aggregated census data and

victimization survey results from the Crime Survey for England and Wales to create a pseudo-population that resembles the demographic characteristics of the residents of Manchester. Researchers combined this information with police-recorded crime data and victim surveys for the region to simulate reported and unreported crime incidents. The authors applied GIS software and statistical analysis to evaluate differences in police data at various levels of geographical aggregation – Output Areas, Lower Super Output Areas, Middle Super Output Areas, and Wards.

Buil-Gil et al. (2022) determined that police data results in substantially increasing measurement error, especially at fine levels of geographical aggregation. Authors found that police-recorded crime data varied significantly at different levels of address-level resolution and was substantially lower than expected for larger statistical areas. The authors explained that such inconsistencies in police records hinder effective hotspot detection and appropriate resource allocation to modulate crime levels and patterns. Buil-Gil et al. (2022) concluded that while GIS mapping of police data is a critical tool in geographical analysis of crime to inform the most efficient policing strategies, analysts and managers should acknowledge the limitations of police data and apply correction measures to account for recording biases.
Harnessing GIS for Crime Mapping in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review of Applications, Challenges, and Opportunities

Yusuf et al. (2025) demonstrated that Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is a technology that has become crucial in crime mapping because it helps in acquiring, storing, presenting, visualizing, and analyzing crime data relative to geographical space. In their work, Yusuf et al. (2025) explain that geographic information systems help police forces identify hotspots, analyze patterns and clusters, track trends, and allocate

resources efficiently to reduce crime levels. The authors demonstrate that by using the software in analyzing patterns, hotspots, and clusters, police can make evidence-based policing decisions to control and prevent criminal activities. According to the authors, with the rising complexity of crimes and rapid urbanization, GIS has become a crucial tool in combating crime and enhancing security in Sub-Saharan Africa.

Yusuf et al. (2025), in their paper, explain the increasing application of GIS technology in crime mapping in Sub-Saharan Africa, including Nigeria, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, and Zimbabwe. The authors demonstrate the extent to which the technology has been utilized in the region to identify hotspots and clusters and analyze patterns of criminal activities. In Nigeria, for instance, crime mapping using GIS has been applied in Lagos and Abuja to track the situations of crimes and enhance police efficiency. Similarly, in Ethiopia and Zimbabwe, researchers have used GIS software such as ArcGIS, QGIS, and Geoda in analyzing hotspots and employing efficient police beats in the two countries.

In his paper, Yusuf et al. (2025) demonstrate the various applications of GIS in crime mapping, including hotspot analysis, temporal and spatial analysis of police data, and environmental crime analysis. For instance, the authors explain that GIS technology facilitates

-temporal analysis of crime patterns and helps identify relationships between the environment and criminal activities. According to the work, GIS helps track the locations and times of crime patterns, ranging from petty crimes to violent crimes and cybercrimes. The software also aids in analyzing the role of roads, derelict buildings, liquor shops, land use, and other elements in promoting or preventing criminal activities. Moreover, GIS helps in predictive policing by analyzing past incidents of crime, evaluating risks associated with various activities, and predicting future crime trends.

Yusuf et al. (2025) highlight some of the challenges that have hindered the extensive application of GIS technology in crime mapping in developing countries. According to the authors, the application of GIS crime mapping has faced geographical, financial, technical, and human resource challenges. For instance, the lack of good data, geocoding problems, and inadequate technology and expertise contribute to the limited use of the technology in criminology. Additionally, the authors highlight the lack of standardized data management systems, institutional coordination, and professionalism in crime analysis as a major limitation in using GIS technology to combat crimes. According to the work, ethical issues associated with the collection, storage, and use of data pose a significant challenge when applying GIS technology in crime mapping.

Yusuf et al. (2025) performed a systematic review of the application of GIS in crime mapping. The authors conducted a study following the PRISMA guidelines and focused on applications, challenges, and opportunities associated with the use of GIS technology in five electronic databases, namely, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, JSTOR, and PubMed. The initial search resulted in 186 documents, but only 29 studies met the inclusion criteria and were considered for final review and thematic analysis. According to the results, the 29 papers selected represent empirical studies carried out between 2010 and 2025 on the application of GIS in crime mapping. The 29 papers were thematically analyzed according to applications, challenges, and opportunities based on the research questions.

According to the study by Yusuf et al. (2055), GIS has enhanced hotspot identification, enabled predictive policing, and promoted environmental criminology, thus increasing crime prevention and control. The study indicates that even though GIS crime mapping has been associated with various challenges, it has great potential in being integrated

into criminology to transform security sectors across the world. The authors recommend increased investment in GIS technology, building standardized databases, and promoting collaboration in combating crime while developing countries such as those in Sub-Saharan Africa utilize the opportunities offered by the technology to address a wide range of crimes.

planners, policymakers, and law enforcers to ensure safe and sustainable cities through evidence-based and sustainable strategies.

In addition, the researchers highlighted that the modern theories of environmental crime help to focus attention on the importance of the relationship between urban development patterns and the spatial distribution of crime.

They also pointed out that the study of the impact of the environment on criminal behavior is key to crime prevention and control. Dynamic Crime Mapping: Improving the Interpretation of Spatial Crime Patterns

Spencer (2026) pointed out that the use of mapping in crime analysis is an integral part of spatial crime understanding, with most of the studies utilizing mapping being static analyses of crime-and-place. The author stated that dynamic crime mapping helped visualize the patterns through interactive features such as zooming, filtering, selecting layers. Spencer (2026) argued that dynamic visualization enhanced the interpretation of hierarchical, multi-scaled, and time-dependent processes that are key factors in understanding crime concentration and hotspots.

Spencer (2026) demonstrated the historical background of dynamic crime mapping by discussing the evolution of crime mapping through the Cartographic school, the Chicago school, the GIS era, and the current

paradigm. The author showed how improvements in geographic information systems (GIS) advanced spatial crime analyses through hotspot mapping, spatial clustering, and spatial statistics. However, Spencer (2026) noted that many published works on crime mapping still rely on static visuals to interpret spatial patterns and hierarchies.

Spencer (2026) argued that dynamic visualizations offer more advantages than static maps in studying and representing crime-and-place. The author highlighted the benefits of using web-based interactive maps in enabling the simultaneous viewing, filtering, and exploring of spatial patterns at various scales. By using

and other filters, researchers can visualize the patterns and trends of crimes at different scales and levels simultaneously without relying on multiple figures. Such dynamic visualizations help compare patterns and trends between census blocks and census tracts to enhance the understanding of the spatial distribution of crime, concentration, and hotspots. Spencer (2026) stated
that the use of dynamic visualization and interactive features in exploring spatial patterns was an important methodological innovation that enhanced crime science.

Spencer (2026) conducted a scoping review of published works to establish how visualization techniques, especially dynamic and interactive mapping, were used in studying the relationships between crimes and places. The author retrieved 930 publications from the search strategy done in the last five years (2010-2024). From the 930 publications, Spencer (2026) selected 93 publications for the detailed review and analysis of the mapping procedures used. The author found that 77% of the reviewed articles had utilized mapping in their studies, with less than 5% using dynamic visualization techniques. From the analysis, Spencer (2026) established that 62% of the selected publications were appropriate for dynamic mapping visualizations due to their hierarchical nature, temporal aspects, and/or use of overlapping information.

Spencer (2026) demonstrated the application of dynamic crime mapping in a real-world scenario by analyzing the publicly available incident data from the Atlanta Metropolitan Crime Analysis Unit on Georgia. The author created R packages, including Leaflet, Shiny, and

, to make interactive web-based maps for exploring and visualizing the patterns of crimes in Atlanta over the 2015-2019 period at census block and tract levels. Additionally, the use of interactive web-based maps allowed comparing patterns at the two levels simultaneously while highlighting hotspots, differences, and trends and examining the contextual information associated with the location and time of incidents. Spencer (2026) concluded that the use of dynamic mapping visualizations enabled enhanced interpretation of spatial patterns of crime compared to static figures by enabling simultaneous exploration of patterns at multiple levels with just a few clicks.

Spencer (2026) concluded that dynamic crime mapping was a powerful tool in facilitating the visualization, interpretation, and display of complex data patterns in modern crime analysis. The author recommended that criminologists and law enforcement agencies adopt interactive web-based GIS tools, especially in studies exploring hierarchical, time-dependent, and hotspot analyses of the relationships between places and crime. However, Spencer (2026) argued that visualizing and analyzing crime patterns using interactive GIS required ethical considerations in protecting the privacy and security of victims and ensuring confidentiality. As such, the author emphasized the need to consider the relevance and complexity of the data in any visualization process, stating that visualization was not an end-goal but a process. Overall, Spencer (2026) asserted that embracing dynamic web-based GIS visualization would enhance effective crime prevention and control strategies and promote evidence-based policing practices

Kebede et al. (2025) adopted a concurrent mixed method research design to reveal the patterns of crime by
and qualitatively. The authors used Hot spot analysis, Moran’s I Spatial autocorrelation,

Modeling, Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), and Standard Deviation Ellipse (SDE) spatial statistical models. The study adopted descriptive and exploratory sequential procedures to explore the relationships between various factors and crime events and assess the patterns of spatial randomness and non-randomness of the incidents. Kebede et al. (2025) achieved their objective of examining the spatial distribution of 2018-2021 crime incidents in Dessie City by adopting concurrent mixed methods and employing ArcGIS Pro software.

The authors examined the spatial clustering patterns of the identified crime incidents and established that the spatial distribution of incidents was not random. Kebede et al. (2025) revealed that Hote, Arada, and Segno were high-crime hotspots, whereas

were the cold spots in Dessie City. Moran’s I spatial autocorrelation results showed a positive Moran’s Index of 0.380984, an associated z-score of 3.297616, and a p-value of less than 0.01, providing statistically significant evidence that crime incidents occurred non-randomly at a local level. Moreover, the authors established that the majority of the identified crime incidents were related to theft and that the incidents occurred mostly during the day. Kebede et al. (2025) adopted Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation to predict the likely hotspots and

of crime and hypothesized that the central business district of Dessie City would be the next major crime hotspot because of the presence of many businesses, bus stands, markets, and dense populations.

(2025) revealed that most crime incidents exhibited a north-to-south directional distribution, whereas murders showed a northeast-to-southwest directional distribution using Standard Deviation Ellipse analysis. The authors concluded that the use of GIS-based crime mapping approaches in combination with any of the above-mentioned

spatial models can help improve the identification of crime hotspots and patterns, predict future incidents, and enhance spatial crime analysis in general. Kebede et al. (2025) recommend that policing agencies use GIS-based approaches to improve hotspot detection, patrol operations, and resource allocation while promoting effective crime prevention and control

A Spatial Analysis of Crime Trends and Solution Efficiency across Philippine Police Regional Offices

Sangco et al. (2026) performed a national-scale spatial analysis to identify patterns of crime and solution efficiency and their relationship with socio-economic characteristics in the country. The authors’ main point is that addressing the patterns of crime and their solution in the context of both national and international concerns is necessary for the development of effective policing strategies at national administrative levels, especially for the territory as diverse and complex as the Philippines. Previous research attempted to address the issue of identifying hotspots of crime, yet the authors note the absence of nationwide analyses, and they attempt to fill this gap by utilizing GIS and spatial statistical analysis to study the interplay between crimes, their resolution, and socio-economic factors.

Sangco et al. (2026) conducted the study by retrieving crime incident and crime solved records from the Philippine National Police between January 2022 and September 2023. The researchers accessed socioeconomic and demographic data from the Philippines Statistics Authority and the World Bank and regional shapefiles from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX). Sangco et al. integrated the data using GIS software. The researchers used QGIS 3.4, GeoDa, and

to carry out hotspot analysis, Global Moran’s I Spatial Autocorrelation, Spatial Lag Modeling (SPLM), and Spatial Scan Statistics to reveal the hotspots of crimes, assess the association, examine the influence of socio-economic determinants, evaluate the efficacy of solutions, and identify clusters of significantly low values of police regional offices across the country.

According to the study conducted by Sangco et.al in 2026, it was found that there were various categories of crimes including theft, robbery, rape, murder, physical injury, homicide, and carnapping which were reported throughout the duration of the study. However, it was noted that these crimes were not uniformly distributed, instead, hotspots were identified for most of the crimes while some regions had lower instances of criminal activity. The National Capital Region, CALABARZON, Central Luzon, and Central Visayas were found to have the highest occurrences of major crimes such as robbery, theft, rape, and carnapping. In contrast, CAR, MIMAROPA, and BARMM were determined to be less criminal due to their lack of substantial urban development. It was concluded by the researchers that highly urbanized and developed areas offer more opportunities for individuals to commit crimes due to the increased level of interactions taking place in these regions.

Sangco et al. (2026) utilized Global Moran’s I Spatial Autoregression in order to determine whether instances of crime were distributed randomly or not. According to the results, there was an occurrence of a positive spatial autocorrelation, which was determined by Moran’s I value of 0.384, p-value of 0.000. This implies that instances of crime were not randomly distributed throughout the regions of the Philippines. Further analysis using the Spatial Lag Model revealed that unemployment and population are positive contributors to the incidence of crime, while the number of police stations is a negative contributor to the incidence of crime, which implies that higher numbers of police stations lead to significantly lower levels of crime.

Sangco et al. (2026) also performed Spatial Scan Statistics in order to detect the existence of statistically significant low-risk (cold spot) clusters. As a result, three large low clusters were identified, which were significantly lower than the expected number of incidents. The researchers concluded that the detected areas had a considerably low risk level compared to the

neighboring sites. Overall, the authors highlight the importance of combining GIS, hotspot mapping, spatial autocorrelation, spatial regression, and spatial clustering analysis to study patterns of crime and police performance adequately. The researchers recommended focusing on improving police activity in high-crime urban settings, increasing the level of community policing and interagency cooperation, and promoting educational and employment opportunities as the key measures to improve
the current state of affairs in the Philippines.

The reviewed literature and related studies reveal that advances in developing GIS for crime analysis are apparent in its spatial accuracy, predictability, artificial intelligence utilization, web accessibility, and theoretical soundness. Foreign studies focus on explainable predictions, enhanced hotspot analysis, and interactive web mapping, as well as implementing machine learning, environmental design theories, and other crime prevention tactics. Local studies centered on the need for applying GIS for effective law enforcement, allocating resources, and engaging communities in public safety across the country. GIS-based crime analysis is still constrained by data discrepancies, biases, inconsistencies, and limited application of spatial analysis in local communities.

The reviewed literature provides substantial theoretical and methodological basis for developing GIS-based crime analysis in improving hotspot identification, spatial accuracy, and community engagement in local government units (LGUs).
et al. (2025), Morgan et al. (2022), and

(2021) agree that criminal activity has spatial patterns that can be predicted using environmental, social, and demographic variables and theories such as Environmental Criminology, Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, Routine Activity, and Social Disorganization.

and Colak (2023) improved the accuracy of spatial analysis using machine learning algorithms in Random Forest Regression and Support Vector Regression, achieving a 78% prediction accuracy in determining the environmental factors for burglaries. Meanwhile, Azis et al. (2021) utilized K-Medoids clustering in unsupervised machine learning to identify spatial patterns associated with high and low-crime locations, and Du and Ding (2023) provided an extensive list of
-temporal prediction models such as Kernel Density Estimation and Risk Terrain Modeling. Karmakar (2024) discussed spatial statistics, including
and Optimized Hot Spot Analysis, and Kebede et al. (2025) analyzed

-temporal patterns of crimes using similar software in Dessie City, Ethiopia. They found that the study area had significant spatial clustering of incidents, and interpolation methods accurately predicted potential crime areas.

Various studies tried to enhance hotspot determination, visualization, and accessibility in developing crime-mapping systems and solutions. Kim et al. (2025) employed Explainable Artificial Intelligence in creating an accessible web-based system that utilizes extreme gradient boosting and SHAP values to explain the model and provide insights into the identified environmental and urban factors affecting criminal activity. Cafaro et al. (2026) proposed a hotspot detection framework that uses a Weighted Fuzzy C-Means clustering algorithm that considers the density of data points and improves the accuracy of the conventional clustering approach while maintaining a short computation time. On the other hand, Spencer (2026) argued that using dynamic and interactive web-based mapping visualization tools is better than static images because it allows multi-scale analysis to understand the changing patterns of crime over time.

However, several studies identified limitations and challenges in implementing GIS-based crime analysis systems and solutions. Yusuf et al. (2025) conducted a systematic review of published literature on the application of GIS in enhancing crime analysis in sub-Saharan Africa and found significant research gaps in the region, such as the lack of standardized geocoding processes and proper infrastructure and expertise in utilizing GIS technology. Similarly, Buil-Gil et al. (2022) found that recording and reporting biases affect the accuracy of micro-area analysis and hotspot identification in several European countries. The findings of Yusuf et al. (2025) and Buil-Gil et al. (2022) can be used as a critical consideration in this study since several LGUs in the Philippines also experience similar issues in adopting GIS-based crime analysis.

Studies conducted in the Philippines to improve community safety and public security through GIS-based solutions highlight the need to develop an accessible system that can maximize the use of existing tools while addressing the limitations of current practices.

(2025) used QGIS in analyzing and visualizing the hotspots and crime trends in Apayao Province to determine the best locations for installing closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras. The study achieved positive feedback from the community as it increased the rate of crime clearance and solution after the installation of CCTV devices based on the recommendations of the analysis. Sangco et al. (2026) performed a spatial analysis of intentional crime incidence in the Philippines using QGIS, GeoDa, and

software. They found that the country exhibits positive spatial autocorrelation across all regions, with theft being the most prevalent type of offense, affecting densely populated areas with a high unemployment rate. Lastly, Laurena et al. (2022) designed a web-based citizen-initiated incident reporting and tracking system using Google Maps API that provides the public with a platform to report crime and track the progress of their reports. The system received positive feedback from the citizens and LGUs due to its convenience and accessibility.

Based on the reviewed literature, several similarities can be drawn among the studies in terms of objectives, research questions, methodology, and scope. Most of the foreign studies mentioned above employed similar hotspot detection and identification technologies, including spatial statistics, machine learning clustering algorithms, and web-based visualization techniques. Some of these studies utilized related crime theories, particularly the application of Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design in addressing community safety issues. Others built upon the findings of previous studies, such as those conducted by Yusuf et al. (2025) and Buil-Gil et al. (2022), by including data bias as one of the variables

affecting crime patterns and integrating it into their analysis. On the other hand, Spencer (2026) focused on creating an interactive, multi-scale mapping application that could better display the analysis results to the users than the static visuals produced by most GIS software.

The reviewed foreign literature and related studies present several limitations and recommendations for future research on GIS-based crime analysis. Most of the studies conducted abroad had a set objective to enhance hotspot identification, making the results too specific to determine the broader impact of utilizing GIS in improving areas related to community safety, law enforcement, and crime prevention. Most of these studies came from countries with better technology and resources in adopting GIS than the Philippines, making them difficult to implement in local government units. The findings of Yusuf et al. (2025) and Buil-Gil et al. (2022) can partially apply to the Philippine setting since some LGUs face similar challenges in adopting GIS-based crime analysis systems. However, the studies made specific recommendations based on the unique needs of their countries, which may not be cost-effective when applied to the Philippines. Most foreign studies focused only on one aspect of GIS-based crime analysis, such as enhancing hotspot identification and applying it to a particular region. There is a need to develop a system or framework that integrates different analyses and makes it accessible to the general public and local government units in terms of cost and complexity.

Based on the research gap identified in the reviewed literature and related studies, this study aims to propose a GIS-Based Integrated Crime Mapping and Analysis System that local government units can utilize in addressing community safety and crime prevention issues. The suggested system should be able to provide spatial information, identify hotspots efficiently and effectively, perform fundamental predictive analysis, and manage incident data while being accessible to the public in terms of its

web and mobile-based interface. Furthermore, implementing this study will ensure that citizens can report incidents conveniently while addressing the issues affecting the accuracy of data and records in current practices and fully utilizing the theories and principles related to crime prevention through environmental design.
Overview of Current Technologies to be Used in the System

The Web-Based Crime Mapping System will use PHP, Laravel, and MySQL as the core technologies for developing the web-based platform. HTML, Tailwind CSS, and JavaScript will be used to create a responsive and user-friendly interface, while Leaflet.js and OpenStreetMap will provide interactive map visualization and geospatial crime mapping features. The system will support crime incident recording, blotter workflow tracking, crime location plotting, barangay visualization, hotspot monitoring, analytics, evidence management, audit logging, and report generation. Visual Studio Code, Composer, Node.js,

, and XAMPP will be used for development, dependency management, and local testing. These technologies were selected to provide secure data management, reliable database storage, accurate map visualization, efficient crime monitoring, and a maintainable web-based application for authorized law enforcement and LGU users.
